question: How does this get to orbit, and what spacecraft does it need?
title: Space Launch and Satellites: A Practical Reference
lede: Launch used to be the constraint. A kilogram to low Earth orbit now costs around $3,000 on a Falcon 9, several times less than a Western expendable rocket charged fifteen years ago, and the hard problems have moved to picking an orbit, building spacecraft at rate, and getting spectrum and ground time. This guide covers {{N_ENTRIES}} launch vehicles, orbits, spacecraft buses, payload types, ground systems, and in-space services, with the mass, cost, and maturity behind each choice.

facets.label: Orbit
facets.tip: Where the option operates, serves, or delivers. LEO = 160–2,000 km, including very low orbits under 350 km · SSO = the sun-synchronous subset near 97–99° inclination that most imaging flies · MEO = 2,000–35,000 km, in practice 8,000 km and 20,200 km · GEO = the 35,786 km ring, and the transfer orbits that feed it · Beyond GEO = cislunar, Lagrange points, and escape · Ground = hardware or service that sits on the ground.

facets.label: Mass
facets.tip: Mass class. For a launch vehicle this is payload delivered to low Earth orbit; for a bus, payload, or servicing vehicle it is spacecraft wet mass at launch. Options that span sizes carry a span. Untagged where mass is not the useful measure, which covers the orbits and most of the ground segment.

facets.label: Buyer
facets.tip: Who actually pays, listed only where that customer is a primary source of demand. Commercial = telecom, imagery, and consumer services sold on the open market · Civil = government agencies buying operational services such as weather, aviation, and disaster response · Science = research missions and exploration programs · Defense & intel = military and intelligence buyers, who pay more for hardening, schedule, and control.

facets.label: Maturity
facets.tip: How settled the option is as a purchase. Routine = many units flying and usually several suppliers, so buying it is a catalog decision · In service = operational, but with one dominant supplier or a thin track record · Emerging = first units flying or first missions under contract · Development = funded and building, nothing operational yet.

facets.label: Cost
facets.tip: Directional cost to field one unit: one launch, one spacecraft, one terminal, one servicing mission. For an orbit it is the all-in cost of putting one useful operational spacecraft there, launch included. Constellation and program totals run far higher and are given in the entries instead.
